title: DUP leader on Article 2, Dillon and the Windsor Framework: rights, sovereignty and the need for clarity
label: 17 September 2026 · Article 2 / Windsor Framework
summary: Gavin Robinson, DUP leader, told the Lords Northern Ireland Scrutiny Committee he thinks Article 2 of the Windsor Framework was unnecessary, has damaged unionist confidence in the Belfast agreement by undermining consent and Northern Ireland’s place in the UK, and that the Supreme Court’s Dillon judgment narrowed but did not resolve the legal uncertainty. He urged the UK Government to state clearly—ideally in Parliament—how Article 2 should operate, warned against a lasting 'rights border' between Northern Ireland and Great Britain, and doubted that a simple explainer or postscript will stop further legal or political disputes.

glossary.definition: The clause in the Windsor Framework that promises 'no diminution of rights' for people in Northern Ireland compared with 2020.
A UK–EU arrangement that changed how Northern Ireland trades and which included Article 2 on rights.
Also called the Good Friday Agreement; the 1998 peace deal that set Northern Ireland's constitutional arrangements and protections.
A UK Supreme Court ruling that limited some interpretations of Article 2 but left wider questions unresolved.
The idea that Northern Ireland keeps following certain EU rules as they change over time.
Sanitary and phytosanitary rules—standards for food safety and animal/plant health used in trade.
A government document explaining how it interprets parts of the Windsor Framework; used by courts and committees.
Independent commission or process mentioned in the transcript relating to dealing with the past (used as referenced; not fully defined in evidence).

chapters.title: Why Article 2 was included — and why the DUP opposes it
chapters.takeaway: Gavin Robinson says Article 2 was unnecessary, politically motivated, and has caused harm to unionist confidence by altering Northern Ireland’s constitutional standing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Gavin, please introduce yourself briefly for the record and make any opening remarks.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: I'm Gavin Robinson, leader of the DUP and MP for Belfast, formerly on European scrutiny committees. I welcome this detailed scrutiny of Article 2 and the Windsor Framework.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want to start by asking why Article 2 was negotiated and what its political significance is.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: I don't believe Article 2 was necessary. It was negotiated to calm fears that I think were politically motivated and misplaced about rights being lost after Brexit.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Rights in Northern Ireland were already protected by domestic law and the Belfast agreement's commitments. Adding Article 2 created an impression of a special legal relationship with the EU that unionists never supported.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Politically, it backfired: meant to protect rights, it has weakened unionist confidence in Northern Ireland's place in the UK and in the consent principle of the Belfast agreement.

chapters.title: Impact on the Belfast agreement and sovereignty
chapters.takeaway: Robinson argues Article 2 risks creating a 'rights border' and undermines the Belfast agreement's consent and constitutional settlement.

turns.speaker: Lord Dodds of Duncairn
turns.text: You say Article 2 breaches the Belfast agreement. Which parts specifically concern you?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: The Belfast agreement rests on Northern Ireland's place in the UK unless people consent otherwise. Article 2, by elevating protections tied to EU standards and being applied without unionist consent, undermines that consent and constitutional clarity.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: It has damaged political stability here; for unionists it looks like decisions about our rights may be taken by others outside the UK framework.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You accept UK parliamentary sovereignty, but want Parliament to respect the Belfast agreement as an international treaty that shaped the settlement?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Yes. I don't claim Northern Ireland sovereignty. I expect the UK Parliament to consider the Belfast agreement—an international treaty—when making changes that affect Northern Ireland's constitutional position.

chapters.title: The Dillon judgment and the search for legal clarity
chapters.takeaway: Dillon narrowed some interpretations of Article 2, but Robinson says it didn't remove serious uncertainty; he wants Parliament and government to state their interpretation clearly, possibly by legislation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Foster of Aghadrumsee
turns.text: Victims' groups point out some rights weren't in place in 2020—so 'no diminution' is unclear. How do you see the Dillon judgment?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Dillon helped by narrowing vague claims, but it's partial. It tackled some expansionist readings, yet left many questions about what counts as 'no diminution' and which rights are in scope.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ludford
turns.text: How should we get more clarity—another government explainer or something stronger?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: An explanatory note won't be enough. Courts will keep being asked to interpret Article 2. I think the Government should make a clear declaratory statement in Parliament, and if needed legislate, to limit Article 2's scope.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Government post-scripts won't bind judges; Parliament needs to be clearer about intention so courts and departments know how to apply the law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Foster of Aghadrumsee
turns.text: Some groups say Dillon doesn't help victims who never had certain rights—how does that fit?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: There are different legal and moral definitions of 'victim' for different processes. We mustn't assume one legal definition covers every claim; many of these issues are political as well as legal.

chapters.title: Everyday effects, dynamic alignment and political choices
chapters.takeaway: Robinson described practical problems from the Framework, warned a 'reset' that aligns Great Britain to the EU could be temporary, and said limited engagement with ministers leaves uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Baroness Sanderson of Welton
turns.text: Do people in Northern Ireland understand Article 2? Are fears real even if people can't name the clause?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Many ordinary people feel they're treated differently: goods not available, firms filling forms to ship within the UK, public items not deliverable to Northern Ireland. They may not cite Article 2, but they feel unequal treatment.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: This isn't just theoretical: product-safety rules have made posting items across the UK harder—for customers and small businesses in Northern Ireland.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick
turns.text: How can rights for all be protected given differing views here?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: The Belfast agreement can accommodate competing aspirations, but the government must not accept measures that, in practice, reduce the rights or status of unionists within the UK without proper consent.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Ballinamallard
turns.text: Post-Dillon, how should government and the Executive meet rights obligations and avoid creating new injustices?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: The UK must assert that its courts interpret UK law and Parliament can legislate uniformly. Right now there's confusion about whether Westminster can act without external constraints: that must be settled clearly.

turns.speaker: Lord Dodds of Duncairn
turns.text: About a 'reset' that aligns Great Britain: how reliable is that as a solution for Northern Ireland?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: A reset that makes Great Britain match EU rules might relieve some friction, but it's fragile: a future UK government could reverse it, leaving Northern Ireland back where it is now—and it also risks sowing resentment in other UK nations forced to follow.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Also, 'separate but equal' arrangements for Northern Ireland are unacceptable—the analogy to outdated US segregation shows why.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are Northern Ireland parties being consulted on the reset?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: My contact with ministers has been limited: a monthly catch-up with the relevant minister previously, some discussions with the Windsor Framework team, but no detailed engagement with the Secretary of State on these issues since his appointment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If this committee concluded Article 2 was redundant and should be repealed, how would people here react?

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Unionists would welcome it enthusiastically. But I expect other parties to resist; they may not engage with the committee's work unless it suits them politically.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Ultimately, the Government must be clearer, act through Parliament if necessary, and restore confidence that Northern Ireland's place in the UK is not being eroded by external interpretation of rights.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We must close now; you'll receive the transcript for correction.

turns.speaker: Rt Hon Gavin Robinson MP
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate the scrutiny and hope it leads to clearer government action.
